⟦300⟧The stress which acts on any plane surface AB (fig. 27), such as an imaginary cross-section of a strained piece, may be represented
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{sc|Fig.}} 27.}}
by a figure formed by setting up ordinates A<math>a</math>, B<math>b</math>, &c., from points on the surface, the length of these being made proportional to the intensity of stress at each point. This gives an ideal solid, which may be called the stress figure, whose height shows the distribution of stress over the surface which forms its base. A line drawn from <math>g</math>, the centre of gravity of the stress figure, parallel to the ordinates A<math>a</math>, &c., determines the point <math>c</math>, which is called the centre of stress, and is the point through which the resultant of the distributed stress acts. In the case of a uniformly distributed stress, <math>ab</math> is a plane surface parallel to AB, and <math>c</math> is the centre of gravity of the surface AB. When a bar is subjected to simple pull applied axially—that is to say, so that the resultant stress passes through the centre of gravity of every cross-section—the stress may be taken as (sensibly) uniformly distributed over any section not near a place where the form of the cross-section changes, provided the bar is homogeneous in respect of elastic quality and is initially in a state of ease and the stress is within the limits of elasticity.

⟦1000⟧''Uniformly Varying Stress.''—Uniformly varying stress is illustrated by fig. 28. It occurs (in each case for stresses within the elastic
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{sc|Fig.}} 28.}}
limit) in a bent beam, in a tie subjected to non-axial pull, and in a long strut or column where buckling makes the stress become non-axial. In uniformly varying stress the intensity <math>p</math> at any point P is proportional to the distance of P from a line MN, called the neutral axis, which lies in the plane of the stressed surface and at right angles to the direction AB, which is assumed to be that in which the intensity of stress varies most rapidly. There is no variation of stress along lines parallel to MN. If MN passes
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{sc|Fig.}} 29.}}
through C, the centre of gravity of the surface, as in fig. 29, it may easily be shown that the total pull stress on one side of the neutral axis is equal to the total push stress on the other side, whatever be the form of the surface AB. The resultant of the whole stress on AB is in that case a couple, whose moment may be found as follows. Let <math>d\text{S}</math> be an indefinitely small part of the surface at a distance <math>x</math> from the neutral axis through C, and let <math>p</math> be the
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{sc|Fig.}} 30.}}
intensity of stress on <math>d\text{S}</math>. The moment of the stress on <math>d\text{S}</math> is <math>xpd\text{S}</math>. But <math>p = p_1x/x_1 = p_2x/x_2</math> (see fig. 29). The whole moment of the stress on AB is <math>\int xpd\text{S} = (p_1x_1)\int x^2d\text{S} = p_1\text{I}/x_1</math> or <math>p_2\text{I}/x_2</math>, where I is the moment of inertia of the surface AB about the neutral axis through C.

⟦2200⟧A stress such as that shown in fig. 28 or fig. 30 may be regarded as a uniformly distributed stress of intensity <math>p_0</math> (which is the intensity at the centre of gravity of the surface C) and a stress of the kind shown in fig. 29. The resultant is <math>p_0\text{S}</math>, where S is the whole area of the surface, and it acts at a distance CD from C such that the moment <math>p_0\text{S}.\text{CD} = (p_2 - p_0)\text{I}/x_1 = (p_1+p_0)\text{I}/x_2</math>. Hence <math>p_2 = p_0(1+x_2\text{S}.\text{CD}/\text{I})</math>, and <math>p_1 = p_0(1-x_1\text{S}.\text{CD}/\text{I})</math>.
